props.title: Ali
props.initialSlug: Will Smith embodies boxing legend Muhammad Ali

sections.content: Ali (2001) stands as Michael Mann's masterful portrait of Muhammad Ali during his defining decade (1964-1974). Will Smith transforms completely, capturing Ali's poetic swagger and principled defiance. The film opens with a bravura sequence cutting between Sam Cooke performing and Ali (then Cassius Clay) training - establishing the rhythm that drives the whole film. Mann frames Ali's story against the turbulent 60s: his conversion to Islam, friendship with Malcolm X (Malcolm X (1992) would later give this relationship even more depth), and refusal to be drafted into Vietnam. The boxing sequences, especially the "Rumble in the Jungle" against George Foreman, deliver visceral intensity through Mann's signature digital photography.

sections.content: Mann's approach to sports biopics influenced later films like Moneyball (2011) and 42 (2013) - focusing on defining moments rather than cradle-to-grave storytelling. The film excels in showing how Ali's personal journey mirrored America's social upheaval. Mann and cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki create a documentary feel while maintaining stunning composition, especially in the quiet moments between fights. The supporting cast delivers remarkable depth: Jamie Foxx as cornerman Drew Bundini Brown, Jon Voight's transformative Howard Cosell, and Jeffrey Wright's complex Louis Farrakhan.

The film's handling of Ali's religious conversion and political awakening set a new standard for sports biopics, later seen in films like The Hurricane (1999) and Creed (2015). Mann resists typical biopic tropes, instead creating an intimate portrait of a man wrestling with identity, faith, and principle during seismic cultural shifts. The film's sound design deserves special notice - mixing period music, fight crowds, and Ali's own words into a rhythmic tapestry that underscores his poetic nature. sections.content: Ali redefined how filmmakers approach sports legends, influencing works like 42 (2013) and Race (2016). Rather than mythologizing their subjects, these films examine how athletes navigate broader social movements. Mann's decision to focus on Ali's most controversial decade - including his Supreme Court battle over conscientious objector status - created a template for examining athletes as cultural figures, later seen in documentaries like The Last Dance (2020).
